Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for the run chase. The umpires and the players are out in the middle. The good sign for South Africa Women is that Sune Luus is padded up and is ready to open up with Laura Wolvaardt. Sophie Molineux to start with the new ball for the Aussies. Let's go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

How might the surface play in the chase? Julia Price is inspecting the pitch at the halfway mark in this contest and reports that the light roller is being rolled in to get a bit of life into the pitch. Informs that it kept low from the James Anderson end and points out that Ismail particularly wasn't able to generate enough bounce from this end. Reckons that chasing 173 on a slow and low pitch is going to be a tough gig against the pacers with the spinners also expected to play a key role later on.

Disciplined Proteas bowling - South Africa's bowling unit put on a highly disciplined performance for most of the contest, refusing to let the game slip away. Nonkululeko Mlaba, Nadine De Klerk and Ayabonga Khaka led the charge with two wickets each, while the rest of the attack chipped in with a wicket apiece, barring Chloe Tryon, who went wicketless. While this target is not overly massive, it remains deeply challenging. The Proteas boast a formidable batting line-up, but face an elite Australian bowling attack that possesses the world-class quality to defend any total.

A quick word from Phoebe Litchfield - On her approach with the bat, she says facing two world-class bowlers meant she couldn't afford to let them dictate, so she looked to attack them. On whether playing here before helps, she feels the wicket played nicely, even though they lost a couple of early wickets, adding she had good memories from playing The Hundred at this ground. About the total, she calls it really competitive, noting the pitch is playing a few tricks. She praises Mlaba's bowling and backs Australia's own spinners to do their job, adding that with a good batting effort behind them, it's now about bowling and fielding well to defend the total.

Middle-order rebuild - The momentum shifted quickly just after the Powerplay when Litchfield departed immediately after raising a brilliant half-century, and the Aussies suffered a double blow by losing Ashleigh Gardner in quick succession. Georgia Wareham then walked out to join a determined Perry, and the duo counter-attacked with a fighting 58-run partnership that pushed Australia into a highly commanding position. Both Perry and Wareham registered valuable contributions in the 30s to back up Litchfield's top score of 50. Despite a decent finish, Australia might feel they left a few runs out on the field as the regular fall of wickets repeatedly halted their charge toward a massive total.

Phoebe's Powerplay blitz - Australia Women finished their 20 overs with a competitive score of 172/8 on the board, largely built on an explosive start from their young opener. By the end of the Powerplay, the Aussies raced to 52 for 2, with Phoebe Litchfield doing the absolute bulk of the damage by smashing 42 of those runs. It wasn't a happy outing for Georgia Voll and Beth Mooney, both of whom fell for single-digit scores inside the first six overs. However, Ellyse Perry joined Litchfield to steady the ship, stitching together a crucial 37-run partnership for the third wicket that set the stage for the team’s power-hitters to launch from.

A yorker, right at the stumps and clocked at 102.3 kph. Garth jams her bat down and appears to have got an inside edge onto her pads, but De Klerk goes up in an appeal for LBW. The umpire turns it down, and South Africa send it upstairs. UltraEdge shows a clear inside edge. The ball deflects off Garth's leg towards backward point, and the batters cross for a single. Australia Women finish on 172/8!

Commentary.Commentary: Right then, we are done with the pre-match formalities. The South African women have huddled near the fence before they take their respective field positions. Georgia Voll and Beth Mooney open up for the Australia Women. Marizanne Kapp has the new ball in hand and is raring to go. Let's play...

Time for the national anthems - We are all set for the action to begin. The flags of both nations have been unfurled. Both sides, along with the match officials, stride out in the middle and line up for their respective national anthems. It will be South Africa's national anthem first, followed by that of Australia.

Australia's star all-rounder is up for a chat - Ellyse Perry, on being part of another World Cup, says she's just excited for the chance to play another edition, adding that it keeps getting bigger each time, which is great for women's cricket. On Australia not being the defending champions, she notes every edition is a clean slate for every team, coming after a two-year gap. She points to the strength across the competition and reckons it's never just about winning or defending a title, it's about playing good cricket. About their opponents, South Africa, she admits they have amazing depth and proven performers, adding that the practice matches against them showed just how real a threat they are. On facing Shabnim Ismail, she calls her a real competitor who brings plenty of energy and pace, and says it's always a nice contest whenever she's in the mix.

PITCH REPORT - Nasser Hussain is pitchside and says not a lot has changed from the first game, and in fact, he reckons that it has gotten a lot brighter with a strong breeze sweeping across. About the dimensions, he informs that there is just 1 meter difference between the square boundaries, with one measuring 60 meters, and the other, 61 meters, while it is 70 meters down the ground. Julia Price joins him and highlights that Scotland batted really well in the first game, though she believes they may have left a few runs, suggesting this could be a 180-plus surface. Calls it a very good pitch with plenty of grass cover. She credits Scotland's bowlers for shutting down the chase by pulling their lengths back. Highlights that Ireland bowled fuller, around the four metre mark, while Scotland's spinners operated quicker, closer to 4.8 metres, with spinners picking up six wickets between them in the second innings. She also points out the breeze caused trouble for the pace bowlers, adding to the variety on show. With Australia fielding four spinners of their own, she expects spin to play a big role as two heavyweight sides square off on a pitch she rates highly.

The captain of South Africa Women - Laura Wolvaardt says she doesn't mind bowling first as her side has a very good record chasing. Laura adds that they have got a good bit of prep heading into this game and a better idea of the conditions as well. Wolvaardt admits that it has been a really tough job picking 11 from the bunch of 15, but the team management has done well to get the best possible XI. Laura adds that Shabnim Ismail is back in the mix and the way she has been working in the buildup to the tournament, it never felt that she had left, and there is a lot of hope resting on her shoulders.

The captain of Australia Women - Sophie Molineux says that they are going to bat first. Adds that the pitch is on the slower side, so they will put the pressure on the opposition later. She reckons that their warm-up matches went well. She ends by saying that the pitch suits her and that she is loving every moment and every challenge of being the captain of their side.

South Africa Women (Playing XI) - Laura Wolvaardt (C), Sune Luus, Annerie Dercksen, Nadine De Klerk, Marizanne Kapp, Chloe Tryon, Kayla Reyneke, Sinalo Jafta (WK), Shabnim Ismail, Nonkululeko Mlaba and Ayabonga Khaka.

Australia Women (Playing XI) - Beth Mooney (WK), Georgia Voll, Phoebe Litchfield, Ellyse Perry, Ashleigh Gardner, Georgia Wareham, Annabel Sutherland, Nicola Carey, Sophie Molineux (C), Kim Garth and Alana King.

TOSS - The two captains are out in the middle for the coin flip. It's a bit windy and overcast out there, but not threatening at all. The flip lands in favor of the Aussies. Australia Women have opted to BAT first.

Aussies thrive away, Proteas struggle - While there are still a few minutes to go for the toss, we have another staggering stat out. Australia have been near unstoppable on the road in women's T20Is lately, winning 15 of their last 16 away games, with six straight wins to their name. The lone blemish came against South Africa, in that 2024 semi-final clash. South Africa, on the other hand, have struggled away from home, winning just once in their last seven T20Is abroad, an 18-run win over New Zealand back in March. Since then, it's been three defeats on the trot.

Scots trump the Irish - As you all know, it's a triple-header Saturday, and we have the result of the first game of the day. Scotland Women have defeated Ireland Women by 40 runs at this very venue in Manchester. Kathryn Bryce, the Scotland skipper, stood out with her all-round performance and deservedly won the POTM award as well for scoring a quickfire 60 (39) in the first innings, and picking up a miser 2-wicket haul in the second innings. As they say, firsts are always sweet. This is the first-ever T20 World Cup win for Scotland. A proud moment for the nation, indeed.

A bit of unfamiliarity - Here's a fun fact for you all. Despite being two of the most well-travelled sides in women's cricket, neither Australia nor South Africa have ever played a T20I at Old Trafford. Two heavyweight nations, a venue steeped in cricket history, and yet this will be a first examination for both at this venue. Whatever the conditions throw up, both sides will be starting from scratch, and that little bit of unpredictability could end up shaping how this contest unfolds. Toss and teams coming up very shortly. Stay tuned.

Aim to erase the 'perpetual challengers' tag - South Africa's overall record at the Women's T20 World Cup doesn't exactly scream dominance, with more losses than wins at 18-21. But recent form tells a different story. They've won three of their last four bilateral series, including a statement 4-1 thrashing of India at home. The squad itself is packed with experience, built around players who have been fixtures across the last several ICC events. The pieces all seem to be in place. The batting order is loaded with players capable of winning games on their own, the bowling attack offers plenty of variety, and the fielding has been consistently sharp. The only thing missing is the one thing that's eluded them for years, turning all that quality into an actual world title.

Kangaroos are eager to hop high again - There's no debating Australia's status as the most successful side in the limited-overs format. But for the first time since 2017, they head into a major tournament with no global title to defend. The T20 crown, held for three editions running, slipped away in 2024, and a semifinal exit at last year's ODI World Cup only added to the sense that the empire is, for now, without a crown. They still largely retain the core that made them the gold standard in women's white-ball cricket, but there's a fresh feel about this side, with Sophie Molineux now leading the team following Alyssa Healy's retirement. And this is her first big examination as a skipper and would want to pass with flying colors.

The Group of Death - Group A, or Group 1, call it whatever you like, but most agree it's the tougher of the two groups to navigate. Just look at who's in it. Australia and South Africa headline the pack, with India and, to an extent, Pakistan, right on their heels as the closest challengers. With a lineup this stacked, every single point is going to matter, and that makes the opening game massive for both sides. A win here doesn't just bring two points on the board, but it sets the tone, builds momentum, and takes off some of the early pressure heading into the fixtures ahead. Lose, and you're already playing catch-up in a group that offers very little breathing room.

Old wounds, unfinished business - October 17, 2024, Dubai. That’s the date that still stings for Australian cricket. The day their bid for a seventh Women's T20 World Cup title came crashing down at the semifinal stage, courtesy of the Proteas. The wound South Africa left that day hasn't faded, and the Kangaroos will be itching to respond strongly to settle the score. Fast forward to Old Trafford, and these two are set to collide again, this time in the group stage of the 2026 edition. For the Aussies, this is time for payback. For the Saffas, it's a chance to prove that Dubai wasn't a one-off. Hello and welcome to our coverage of match number 3, Australia Women vs South Africa Women ​​​​​​at Manchester. So buckle up, because this has the makings of one of the spiciest contests of the tournament.
... MATCH DAY ...

The Old Trafford challenge - The ICC Women's T20 World Cup 2026 is barely out of the blocks and already serving up a heavyweight clash. The first weekend brings the tournament to Old Trafford, where Group A turns into a genuine title fight from the word go. Australia walk in as six-time world champions, the team that every other side measures itself against, the gold standard of white-ball cricket. South Africa walk in as serial finalists, having reached the title clash the last two times around and proven they have what it takes to go the distance. A new captain, a new chapter - This World Cup marks the start of life after Alyssa Healy for Australia. With the veteran wicketkeeper having called time on her international career, the responsibility of steering this dominant side into a new era now rests with left-arm orthodox spinner Sophie Molineux, leading Australia at a T20 World Cup for the first time. Ashleigh Gardner and Tahlia McGrath have been named as her dual deputies, rounding out a fresh look leadership group. For Molineux herself, this tournament also marks a return. A back injury kept her out for much of the Caribbean tour, but she eased back into things in style during last week's unofficial warm-ups against South Africa. With Old Trafford traditionally a happy hunting ground for spinners, the skipper will fancy her chances of making an immediate impact with both bat and ball in hand. Plenty of options in bowling - Australia's selectors clearly weren't shy about making a few bold calls while finalising their squad of fifteen. The headline pick is left-arm pacer Lucy Hamilton, who walks into an attack already stacked with the experience of Kim Garth and Megan Schutt, a decision that screams conditions-first thinking and adds a fresh angle to the new ball options. With just one T20I to her name so far, Hamilton will be eager to make her mark on the big stage and prove her credentials. And leading that pace charge is Annabel Sutherland, the side's leading wicket-taker in the format since the last T20 World Cup, while the likes of Nicola Carey, McGrath and of course, Perry, remain reliable hands to call upon whenever needed. All of which only highlights just how deep Australia's bowling resources really run. The XI picks itself, mostly - Most of Australia's lineup writes itself. The top five only needs Phoebe Litchfield to put the quad concern that kept her sidelined for both Cardiff warm-ups behind her, and things fall into place batting-wise. Add Kim Garth and Megan Schutt as the new ball pair, and that is eight names sorted before the selectors even break a sweat. The real puzzle lies in the spin department, and it's a good problem to have. Molineux, King, Wareham and Gardner together form one of the most dangerous spin quartets in the competition, yet not everyone can realistically fit alongside the rest of the attack. Throw in Grace Harris as another option, and there are genuinely quality players fighting it out for two spots. Complicating matters further, Gardner and Wareham are Australia's second and third highest wicket takers in T20Is, and both bring genuine runs with the bat as well, making this anything but a straightforward call. Proteas bet on big experience - Three major finals, three near misses. The 2023 T20 World Cup, the 2024 T20 World Cup, and the 2025 ODI World Cup have all ended the same way for South Africa, agonisingly close to glory but without that elusive first ICC trophy in hand. That run of heartbreaks has clearly prompted some serious soul searching, with the Proteas convincing veteran pacer Shabnim Ismail and former skipper Dane Van Niekerk to come out of retirement for one more crack at it. Ismail walked away from international cricket after the 2023 World Cup but never really slowed down, continuing to terrorise batters in franchise leagues around the world at 37. Still capable of touching speeds over 120 kph, her return instantly plugs a pace bowling gap that became glaringly obvious during Marizanne Kapp's extended absence through illness earlier in 2026. Van Niekerk, meanwhile, brings a wealth of experience back into the middle order, giving South Africa some much-needed steel at both ends of the innings. To balance these veteran inclusions, South Africa have integrated young talent, most notably the 20-year-old all-rounder Kayla Reyneke. Reyneke earned her senior World Cup debut following an outstanding breakout domestic and international season. All eyes on the marquees - Some players carry a team's hopes more than others, and in this clash. For South Africa, it's all about Laura Wolvaardt. The captain and opener doesn't just lead the Proteas' run charts over the last five years, she tops them all time, and by a considerable margin. 2026 has been a particularly good year too, with an average of 47.5 in T20Is, highlighted by a sensational home series against India where she struck three fifties and a magnificent century. South Africa's other quiet weapon is Marizanne Kapp. She hasn't bowled much T20 cricket this year, but with 93 international wickets to her name, second only to Ismail in the country's history, her threat level on a good day remains as high as ever. Australia counter with Beth Mooney, who simply hasn't stopped scoring. 2025 saw her finish as Australia's top run getter in T20Is, an insanely unbelievable average of 94.75 across nine innings, including four fifties. She and Ellyse Perry also happen to be the two highest run scorers for Australia in T20 World Cup history among the current squad, a stat that says everything about the experience of walking out to play for the Aussies. Team form (Last 5 Women’s T20I, recent first) AUS-W - WWWLW | SA-W - WLWWW. What to expect? Old Trafford's surface tends to offer good bounce and carry for the seamers with the new ball, but there is always a bit for the spinners as the game wears on, which could play right into the hands of both attacks, given how spin-loaded both teams are. With both teams arriving in good touch and carrying momentum from their recent form, expect very little to separate the two early on. History, though, heavily favours Australia. The head-to-head tally reads a lopsided 9-2 in their favour, with South Africa managing just two wins, both coming in 2024. One of those victories proved especially significant, paving the way for the Proteas to book their spot in the final of the last edition. Will the Aussies make them pay for that one, or can South Africa add another chapter to their growing list of upsets against the six-time champions? Old Trafford could well have the answer.
